newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Phnom Penh likely to seek U.N. help to try Pol Pot.
newsitem.headline: Phnom Penh likely to seek U.N. help to try Pol Pot.

text.p: Cambodia's two prime ministers are likely to ask the United Nations to convene an international tribunal to bring Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot to justice, a U.N. official said on Tuesday.
Thomas Hammarberg, a senior U.N. human rights representative, said: "The important thing is that the international procedure start as soon as possible."

Hammarberg said he had separately met co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen and asked them to make a formal request to the U.N. for international assistance in setting up trials for Pol Pot and others responsible for the 1975-79 "killing fields" reign of terror.
"I have reason to believe...that such a request will be made," said Hammarberg, the special representative of the U.N. secretary-general for human rights in Cambodia.
The once-feared Khmer Rouge is split and Pol Pot is on the run in the north of the country after being deserted by most of his fighters, Ranariddh has said.
About 95 percent of the Khmer Rouge fighters remaining in their northern stronghold of Anlong Veng and a group of rebels with Pol Pot want to join the government, he says.
The Khmer Rouge, under whose rule more than a million Cambodians died from torture, execution, starvation, overwork or disease, have been decimated by thousands of defections since August.
Now the rebels are split over whether to make peace.

The guerrillas have balked at peace before, when they reneged on a 1991 pact meant to end Cambodia's long history of conflict. They have been fighting the coalition government formed after a U.N.-sponsored poll in 1993.
The disintegration of the movement has prompted speculation on whether Pol Pot and others can be brought to justice.
Ranariddh told reporters on Tuesday that he wanted Pol Pot captured alive and tried for his crimes.
Hammarberg said a Cambodian tribunal might be similar to those organised in the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda and therefore could face similar obstacles -- including funding constraints.

"My impression is that there will be a request from here, that it will be taken seriously by the U.N., that there will be discussions within the U.N. and the pressure to respond positively will be strong," he said.
He said the tribunal would not be aimed just the top leaders.
"We're not talking about one or two persons. We're talking about a group -- a fairly large group of individuals," he said.
Even former Khmer Rouge foreign minister Ieng Sary, who received a royal pardon last year after being sentenced to death in 1979, could face trial, Hammarberg said.
"It's not just a question of passing verdicts, but also to establish the full story," he said.
